title: Craftsmen and builders
hookLine: Ramgarhia Sikhs, heirs of builders and carpenters

lines: WHAT HOLDS US UP GOES UNSEEN.
cards: Run a hand along the doorframe of the room you're in. Somebody measured that, cut it, checked it with a level, and fixed it in place, and it's easy to go a lifetime without a thought for them.
So much of what holds us up is like that: beams, stairs, the bench outside the gurdwara where the old men sit. In some cities you'll pass a gurdwara with a sign that says Ramgarhia.
That name has a story behind it, and a trade.

teach.h: A NAME FROM A FORT, A TRADE FROM THE HANDS.
teach.b: Start with the people. Ramgarhia Sikhs trace their families to carpenters, masons, smiths and builders.
Year three told how the name came from the Ramgarhia misl, one of the old bands of Sikh riders, and its leader, Jassa Singh, called Ramgarhia after the fort he held.
So the name remembers a fort; the trade remembers hands that know wood and stone. Now the oldest piece.

teach.h: LALO THE CARPENTER, AND HIS BREAD.
teach.b: The janamsakhis, the stories of Guru Nanak's life, tell of a carpenter named Lalo.
In the story, the Guru stays in Lalo's simple home and eats his plain bread, and turns down a feast from a rich official whose wealth came from squeezing others.
The bread earned by a chisel, the story says, was the honest food. It's a story, told in the old collections. But Lalo isn't only a story.
In the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak speaks a hymn to Lalo by name, during the violence of an invasion, telling him plainly what he has seen.

teach.h: AS THE WORD COMES, SO I SPEAK, LALO.
teach.b: Here's what he tells him, in paraphrase: as the word of the Master comes to me, so I speak it, Lalo. A hymn about where the Guru's words come from, spoken to a carpenter. Sikhs call honest work kirat.
Building a wall straight is kirat. Fixing a hinge properly when nobody will check is kirat.
And now: when Sikh families settled in new countries, some remember builders among them raising gurdwaras with their own hands.
Every one of those doors was measured by somebody.

how: Ramgarhia Sikhs keep the name of the Ramgarhia misl and a memory of craft; in some cities they have their own gurdwaras, open to every Sikh, and Sikhs everywhere tell the story of Guru Nanak and Lalo the carpenter.

o: a rank given to soldiers who built the Sikh forts
a guild that hires out builders for temple work
Sikhs whose families trace back to carpenters and masons

games.q: you're Guru Nanak, traveling. a carpenter offers plain bread. a rich official sends for you to a feast. where do you eat?
o: at the official's feast, to change his heart from inside.
with Lalo the carpenter, on his plain bread.
games.why: in the janamsakhi story he stays with Lalo and eats his bread, honest food earned with a chisel, and turns the feast down.

practice: Look around the room and find one thing somebody made, a shelf, a stair, a chair, and think of the person you'll never meet who cut it and fitted it.

Then think of someone you know who works with their hands, a plumber, a cousin who fixes things, a parent who built something once, and let a plain thank-you take shape. If you pray, you can rest on Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Craftsmen and builders. Ramgarhia Sikhs, who trace their families to carpenters, masons and smiths, and keep a name from the Ramgarhia misl. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi: work, honest labor. kirat karni, earning by honest work, is one of the Sikh pillars.

carryVoice: Your line: builders. Kirat can be as small as a straight nail. Until tomorrow.
